questions.q: What is a "golden path" (or "paved road") in platform engineering?
options: An opinionated, supported, well-documented default way to build and deploy a service that's easy to follow and hard to misuse
The only technically possible way to deploy a service, with no alternative permitted
An unsupported script someone wrote once and never maintained
A rule enforced purely through manual approval gates with no tooling behind it
questions.explain: A golden path has to be opinionated, actively supported by the platform team, and documented well enough to follow without hand-holding — the combination that makes it both easy to follow and hard to misuse.

questions.q: Why does unlimited freedom in how teams deploy services tend to create problems at scale, per this lesson?
options: It automatically increases deployment frequency for every team
It fragments the organization into many bespoke 'snowflake' systems, each expensive to secure, support, and understand in isolation
It has no real downsides once a company passes a certain size
It reduces the total amount of infrastructure the organization has to maintain
questions.explain: At scale, unlimited autonomy doesn't produce many independently-optimal decisions — it produces fragmentation, where each team's setup needs its own mental model, its own security review, and can't be assumed to work like any other.

questions.q: What is the key distinction between a golden path and a mandate, as this lesson frames it?
options: A mandate is optional while a golden path is compulsory
There is no real distinction; the two terms describe the same thing
A golden path is the supported default that stays easiest to follow, but a team can deviate for a real reason — they just take on the support burden the platform was carrying for free
A golden path is always slower to use than building something custom
questions.explain: The asymmetry is the point: supported by default, on your own if you deviate. That's what keeps most teams on the path without anyone having to forbid the alternative outright.

questions.q: Where do well-designed golden paths typically come from, according to this lesson?
options: A single architect's untested personal preference, designed from theory
Patterns and practices that already work well somewhere in the organization, generalized and packaged for everyone else to reuse
Whichever vendor the platform team most recently evaluated
Randomly assigned tooling with no prior track record anywhere in the company
questions.explain: Golden paths are rarely invented from scratch — they're usually a deployment setup or pipeline structure that already worked well for one strong team, generalized so every other team can reuse it.

questions.q: What is one concrete benefit of baking security and compliance controls into a golden path template, per this lesson?
options: It removes the need for any future security review of any kind
It makes every service built on it functionally identical in business logic
It guarantees a service will never need to be updated again
A service built on the golden path inherits those controls automatically, instead of each team re-implementing — or quietly skipping — them on its own
questions.explain: Baked-in guardrails mean the controls travel with the template. A team that uses the golden path gets them by default, rather than being trusted to reproduce them correctly from scratch.
